strengths: The paper addresses a relevant deployment problem: pruning reasoning models can reduce accuracy while increasing generation length and runtime. Calibrating on generated reasoning traces is a simple, practical intervention requiring no retraining.

The strongest results show substantial improvements over both generic C4 and task-specific prompt calibration. At 50% sparsity, 7B MATH500 accuracy improves from 74.4% with C4 and 81.2% with prompts to 90.0% with RAC.

Experiments cover four model sizes on mathematics and three on coding. The reconstruction-error visualization, alternative trace-source comparison, and semi-structured pruning experiments provide useful supporting evidence.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited to changing the calibration data for an existing pruning algorithm. The paper does not adequately establish the value of self-generated traces relative to readily available worked solutions, existing reasoning datasets, or other task-matched completions. Despite claims of broad compatibility, the empirical validation centers on SparseGPT and one distilled Qwen model family.

The coding evaluation is materially ambiguous. Section 5.1 and the discussion define acc@1:16/codegen_pass@1:16 as success anywhere among 16 predictions, which corresponds to pass@16 rather than pass@1 estimated using 16 samples. The paper must clarify the implemented estimator, sampling procedure, and LiveCodeBench version before these results can be interpreted reliably. The description of mathematical evaluation as the 'single most-confident prediction' is also underspecified.

The distribution-matching argument is overstated. RAC collects trajectories under the dense model, whereas deployment uses the pruned model, whose generated prefixes can differ substantially. Figure 2 measures reconstruction on fixed dense-model prefixes and therefore does not establish matching of the compressed model's actual rollout distribution. Furthermore, processing a fixed causal sequence by prefill or decoding does not itself create the claimed distinction; the relevant change is the distribution of token sequences.

The efficiency evidence is incomplete. Hardware, batching, inference backend, sparse kernels, and timing methodology are not reported. Most unstructured-pruning results remain slower than the dense model, and coding results omit dense runtimes. Table 4 lacks a dense FP8 baseline, preventing separation of quantization and sparsity gains. Calibration generation time and memory costs are also unmeasured.

Important reproducibility and experimental controls are missing: calibration prompt counts, sequence packing and truncation, generation settings, pruning hyperparameters, and repeated calibration runs. Although the nominal token budget is matched, these omissions make it difficult to assess the calibration comparison. The abstract announces a code link but supplies none. LiveCodeBench dates and overlap checks against Codeforces calibration data are particularly important.

Several quantitative claims exceed or contradict the evidence. Section 5.2 reports 0.940 accuracy for RAC+FP8 with first-and-last-third pruning, whereas Table 4 reports 0.920; 0.940 belongs to RAC without FP8. Table 4 also reports inconsistent standard errors for identical 0.950 accuracies. The claimed advantage of on-policy traces rests on one model pair, small differences, and no paired significance analysis; off-policy traces actually perform better at 40% sparsity. These issues, together with the evaluation ambiguities, leave the submission below the acceptance threshold despite promising high-sparsity gains.

strengths: RAC is a simple, practically motivated modification to pruning calibration that requires no retraining and fits naturally into SparseGPT.

The reported gains at high sparsity are substantial, including over task-specific prompt calibration. At 50% sparsity, 7B MATH500 accuracy improves from 0.812 with prompt-only calibration to 0.900 with RAC; LiveCodeBench improves from 0.228 to 0.283.

Experiments cover four model sizes for mathematics and three for coding. The reconstruction-error analysis, off-policy comparison, semi-structured pruning experiment, and decoding-budget ablation provide useful supporting evidence.
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily a calibration-data substitution within an existing pruning objective. Given the acknowledged prior work on task-specific calibration and synthetic reasoning traces, stronger controls are needed to establish the distinctive value of self-generated CoT: existing worked solutions, answer-only data, and matched-length off-policy traces are not adequately compared. All evaluated models belong to the same distilled Qwen family, and integration with pruning algorithms beyond SparseGPT is not demonstrated.

The coding evaluation metric is materially ambiguous. Sections 5.1 and 5.2 describe acc@1:16/codegen_pass@1:16 as success anywhere among 16 predictions, which corresponds to pass@16 rather than pass@1 estimated from 16 samples. The manuscript needs to specify the actual estimator, sampling procedure, benchmark version, and evaluated problem count before these results can be interpreted reliably.

The distribution-matching argument is overstated. Dense-model rollouts reproduce the dense policy's activation distribution, not necessarily the pruned model's free-running distribution. Figure 2 evaluates shared dense-model prefixes, so it establishes improved reconstruction under those prefixes rather than reduced error accumulation during autonomous generation. Moreover, processing identical completed sequences with causal teacher forcing would produce equivalent activations; the essential change is the calibration text distribution, not decoding itself.

The efficiency evidence is incomplete. Hardware, inference engine, batching, sparse kernels, timing protocol, and generation-length statistics are unspecified. Most unstructured-pruning configurations remain slower than the dense model. Table 4 provides useful throughput measurements, but lacks a dense FP8 baseline and a complete prompt-only comparison, preventing separation of sparsity, quantization, and calibration effects. Calibration generation time and memory costs are also unmeasured.

Several reporting inconsistencies weaken confidence. Section 5.2 claims 0.940 accuracy for RAC+FP8 with first-and-last-third pruning, whereas Table 4 reports 0.920; 0.940 belongs to RAC without FP8. Table 4 also reports an unexplained standard error of 0.001 for accuracy 0.950, versus approximately 0.010 for comparable results. Claims of consistent superiority are stronger than the tables support, particularly at low sparsity.

Reproducibility and statistical support are insufficient for the stronger claims. Calibration prompt counts, sequence packing/truncation, generation settings, pruning hyperparameters, and calibration-to-test overlap checks are not documented adequately. Reported standard errors do not establish robustness across calibration samples or random seeds. The on-policy advantage rests on one model pairing, reverses at 40% sparsity, and lacks paired significance analysis. These gaps leave a promising empirical observation below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: RAC addresses a relevant problem with a simple, practical modification to calibration that requires no retraining or changes to the underlying pruning algorithm.

The strongest results show substantial improvements beyond domain-specific prompt calibration. At 50% sparsity, 7B MATH500 accuracy increases from 81.2% with prompts to 90.0% with RAC, while evaluation time decreases from 115.6 to 35.3 minutes.
Experiments cover four model sizes for mathematics and three for coding, multiple sparsity levels, and useful extensions involving semi-structured sparsity and decoding budgets.
The held-out activation analysis provides evidence consistent with the proposed mechanism: calibrating on reasoning traces reduces reconstruction error on dense-model continuations.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol has a consequential metric ambiguity. Sections 5.1 and 5.2 describe codegen_pass@1:16 as success anywhere among 16 predictions, which corresponds to pass@16 rather than pass@1 estimated from 16 samples. Sampling, ranking, and aggregation procedures are not specified sufficiently to determine what Table 2 measures.

Reproducibility is inadequate for assessing the reported accuracy and runtime gains. The paper omits the LiveCodeBench version/date range, decoding settings, hardware and inference configuration, and important calibration details such as sequence packing and prompt counts. The abstract announces a code link but provides none.

The contribution is principally a calibration-data change to SparseGPT, and the experiments do not sufficiently isolate its distinctive value. Missing controls include existing reasoning-solution datasets, answer-only calibration, and varying trace length or prompt-to-trace allocation. The single off-policy comparison has small, mixed differences and does not convincingly establish the importance of using the dense model's own traces.

Practical efficiency is only partially established. Most unstructured RAC models remain slower than their dense counterparts. Table 4 lacks dense FP8 and complete matched pruning baselines, preventing separation of sparsity and quantization benefits; calibration-generation time and memory costs are also unmeasured. Moreover, the text claims 0.940 accuracy at 1675 tok/s for RAC+FP8, whereas the table reports 0.920.

The distribution-matching claim is overstated. Dense-model rollouts match the dense policy, not necessarily the compressed model's inference distribution. Figure 2 evaluates shared dense-generated prefixes, so it supports improved reconstruction under those prefixes but does not directly establish reduced error accumulation on the pruned model's own trajectories.

Generality and statistical support remain limited: all models belong to the same Qwen-based distillation family, only SparseGPT is evaluated as the pruning algorithm, and no repeated calibration or decoding runs are reported. Reported standard errors do not establish robustness to those sources of variation. Together with the protocol uncertainties, these gaps leave the promising empirical contribution below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: RAC is a simple, practically useful modification to calibration that requires no retraining and integrates with existing pruning algorithms.
The experimental coverage is substantial: DeepSeek-R1 Qwen and Llama variants, Qwen3, three pruning algorithms, and both mathematics and coding tasks. Benefits are especially clear at high sparsity.

Several improvements are large. At 50% sparsity, DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-7B improves from 81.2% with prompt-only calibration to 90.0% with RAC on MATH500, while evaluation time falls from 115.6 to 35.3 minutes.
The held-out activation analysis, off-policy comparison, decoding-budget experiments, and semi-structured pruning results provide useful evidence beyond headline accuracy.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited to changing the calibration distribution, and differentiation from existing self-calibration and task-specific calibration is not established experimentally. Comparisons against self-calibration, existing reasoning solutions, and task-conditioned non-reasoning completions would clarify whether model-specific CoT generation is essential.

The inference-distribution argument is overstated. Dense-model rollouts match the dense policy, whereas the deployed pruned model can generate different trajectories. Figure 2 measures errors under shared dense-model prefixes, so it does not establish reduced error accumulation along the pruned model’s own trajectories. Moreover, causal processing of calibration text already produces next-token activations; the relevant distinction is the text distribution rather than an intrinsic prefill-versus-decode difference.

The coding metric is materially ambiguous. Section 5.1 defines acc@1:16 as success anywhere among 16 predictions, which corresponds to pass@16, while Table 5 reports pass@1:16. Pass@1 estimated from 16 samples is a different quantity. Sampling settings, the LiveCodeBench version/date range, and evaluation sample counts are insufficiently specified.

Important calibration and reproducibility details are missing: prompt counts, sequence packing and truncation, generation settings, pruning hyperparameters, and calibration runtime and memory. Although the stated token budget is matched, there are no budget or trace-length ablations to separate the effects of reasoning content, sequence length, and prompt diversity.

Deployment-efficiency evidence remains incomplete. Most results concern unstructured sparsity without specifying sparse execution support, and RAC models often remain slower than dense models. Table 6 provides useful 2:4 throughput measurements but lacks a dense FP8 baseline, complete matched prompt-only comparisons, and sufficient serving details to isolate the gains from sparsity and quantization. Section 5.2 also reports 0.940 accuracy for a RAC+FP8 configuration whose table entry is 0.920.

Reported standard errors do not establish robustness across calibration draws or generation seeds. This matters particularly for AIME-25 and the small on-policy versus off-policy differences: off-policy calibration actually performs slightly better at 40% sparsity. Repeated runs and paired comparisons would strengthen these claims.

strengths: RAC addresses a relevant deployment problem with a simple, practical intervention: calibrating pruning on task prompts and model-generated reasoning traces, without retraining.
The empirical coverage is substantial, spanning DeepSeek-R1 Qwen and Llama variants, Qwen3, three reasoning benchmarks, and SparseGPT, ALPS, and WANDA.

Several improvements over domain-matched prompt-only calibration are large. At 50% sparsity, DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-7B improves from 0.812 to 0.900 on MATH500, and Qwen3-8B with ALPS improves from 0.890 to 0.940.
The held-out activation analysis, off-policy comparison, and semi-structured pruning experiments provide useful supporting evidence beyond the main accuracy tables.
weaknesses: The methodological contribution is incremental relative to task-specific calibration and self-calibration, and the closest alternatives are not adequately tested. There is no direct self-calibration baseline or controlled comparison with existing reasoning solutions, answer-only continuations, or length-matched generated text. Consequently, the experiments do not isolate the benefit of on-policy CoT from broader benefits of calibrating on task-relevant solution text.

The evaluation metrics are materially ambiguous. Section 5.1 defines acc@1:16 as success anywhere among 16 predictions, which corresponds to pass@16, whereas Table 5 calls it pass@1:16, potentially meaning pass@1 estimated from 16 samples. These measure different capabilities. Describing mathematical evaluation as the model's 'single most-confident prediction' also leaves the actual decoding procedure unclear.

Reproducibility is insufficient: decoding temperatures, sampling settings, calibration prompt counts, sequence packing and truncation, pruning hyperparameters, LiveCodeBench version/date range, and inference configuration are not specified. Although a 1M-token budget is stated, how prompt-only and RAC datasets are constructed under that budget is unclear. The promised anonymized code link is absent from the supplied manuscript.

The inference-distribution argument is overstated. Dense-model trajectories match the dense policy, not necessarily the compressed model's trajectories after pruning. Figure 2 measures teacher-forced hidden-state error on dense-generated prefixes; it does not establish reduced error under the pruned model's own rollouts. The small on-policy/off-policy comparison also lacks repeated runs supporting its interpretation.

Practical efficiency is not convincingly established. Most results use unstructured sparsity without specifying an accelerated execution backend, and RAC often remains slower than the dense model. Table 6 provides useful hardware-oriented evidence but omits dense-FP8 and unquantized prompt-only controls, preventing clean attribution of speedups. Calibration generation time, memory savings, output-length distributions, and serving settings are not reported.

Reporting inconsistencies and limited uncertainty analysis weaken confidence. Section 5.2 claims 0.940 accuracy for RAC+FP8 with first-and-last-third pruning, while Table 6 reports 0.920. That table also reports an unexplained SE of 0.001 at 0.950 MATH500 accuracy. AIME results have large standard errors, and no repeated calibration or decoding runs establish the stability of smaller gains. Overall, the promising empirical pattern does not yet overcome the baseline, evaluation, and reproducibility gaps required for acceptance.

strengths: RAC addresses a practically important problem with a simple, technically plausible intervention: calibrating pruning on model-generated reasoning traces requires no retraining and integrates directly with existing pruning methods.

The empirical coverage is substantial: DeepSeek-R1 Qwen and Llama variants, Qwen3, three pruning algorithms, and mathematics and coding benchmarks. Including domain-matched prompt-only calibration is a useful control.

Several improvements are large. At 50% sparsity, DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-7B achieves 90.0% MATH500 accuracy versus 81.2% with prompt-only calibration and 74.4% with C4. ALPS experiments provide further evidence that the benefit extends beyond SparseGPT.
The held-out activation analysis supports the proposed mechanism, while the structured-sparsity, off-policy calibration, and decoding-budget experiments provide useful additional perspectives.
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily a calibration-data modification, and its distinction from existing self-calibration is insufficiently demonstrated experimentally. Comparisons against self-calibration and existing domain-specific solution traces are missing; prompt-only baselines do not establish that generating model-specific CoT is necessary.

The coding evaluation is ambiguously specified. Section 5.1 defines acc@1:16 as success anywhere among 16 predictions, which corresponds to pass@16, while Table 5 labels the metric pass@1:16. These differ materially from pass@1 estimated using 16 samples. Sampling settings and the LiveCodeBench version/date range are also missing.

Calibration is not sufficiently reproducible: the manuscript specifies 1M tokens but does not explain prompt counts, sequence packing/truncation, prompt-versus-response allocation, generation settings, or calibration/test deduplication. It also provides no measured calibration cost, despite requiring lengthy model-generated traces. The promised anonymous code link is absent.

The claim that calibration matches the inference-time activation distribution is too strong: traces come from the dense model, whereas the pruned model can generate different prefixes. Figure 2 measures errors under shared dense-model prefixes and therefore does not establish control of errors during the pruned model's own rollouts. The on-policy comparison uses only one model pair, with differences small relative to the reported uncertainty.

Deployment benefits remain incompletely established. Most experiments use unstructured sparsity without documenting sparse execution, memory savings, batching, or inference software. Table 6 offers encouraging 2:4 throughput results but lacks dense-FP8 and prompt-only non-FP8 controls and end-to-end task latency. Section 5.2 also reports 0.940 accuracy for RAC+FP8 where Table 6 gives 0.920.

Reported standard errors do not characterize variation across calibration samples or generation seeds. This matters particularly for the 30-problem AIME benchmark and modest improvements at lower sparsity. Overall, the substantial empirical gains are promising, but the missing comparisons and evaluation ambiguities leave the paper slightly below the acceptance threshold.
